subject: English
topic: Word Swap / Error Spotting in Sentences

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, one word has been used incorrectly. Choose the word that should replace it.

'The principal reason for the delays was that the contractors had underestimated the sheer principal of the project.'

The second 'principal' should be replaced by:

options.option_text: principle (the scale or magnitude of a project is not 'principal' or 'principle'; the correct word for 'scale/magnitude' would be 'scope' — but 'principle' is closest in the swap context)
scope (the second 'principal' is incorrectly used; it should be 'scope' — as in the scope or scale of the project)
priority (changes meaning too far from the original intent)
principle (PRINCIPAL=main/head; PRINCIPLE=rule/belief; neither applies to 'magnitude of a project')

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Principal' means primary or chief (adjective) or head of a school (noun). The second 'principal' is used in place of what should logically be 'scope' (the size/extent of the project). 'Principle' would mean a fundamental rule — also incorrect here. The sentence requires a word describing the magnitude/extent of the project. 'Scope' is the correct replacement.

questions.stem:
Identify the wrongly used word and choose the correct replacement:

'His compliment of the chef's cooking was a genuine reflection of how much he had enjoyed the meal.'

options.option_text: complement (COMPLIMENT = praise; COMPLEMENT = complete/enhance — here 'praise' is correct meaning, so compliment is correct)
No error — 'compliment' is correctly used here (a compliment means an expression of praise)
commendation (changing the word unnecessarily)
complement (the sentence is about praising the chef — 'compliment' is the correct word, not 'complement')

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Compliment' means an expression of praise, admiration, or respect. 'His compliment of the chef's cooking' means his praise for the chef — this is correct in context. There is NO error. 'Complement' would mean something that completes or enhances — not applicable here. This question tests whether students can distinguish COMPLIMENT (praise) from COMPLEMENT (complete).

questions.stem:
One word in the sentence is wrongly used. Choose the correct word to replace it:

'The committee was asked to advice the government on ways to reduce carbon emissions.'

options.option_text: advise (ADVICE=noun; ADVISE=verb; 'to advice' is wrong — the infinitive form needs the verb 'advise')
advices (not a standard English word — 'advice' has no plural)
advising (would change the tense incorrectly)
No error — 'advice' can be used as a verb

questions.explanation: A is correct. ADVICE is a noun (uncountable): 'she gave good advice.' ADVISE is a verb: 'she advised him.' In the sentence 'was asked to [verb]', the infinitive form of the verb is needed. 'To advice' is wrong — 'advice' is not a verb. Correct: 'was asked to ADVISE the government.' This is the classic advice/advise confusion in English grammar.

questions.stem:
One word has been used incorrectly. Replace it:

'She was so effected by the tragedy that she could not speak for several minutes.'

options.option_text: affected (EFFECT=noun/verb meaning 'result/to bring about'; AFFECT=verb meaning 'to influence' — 'effected' should be 'affected')
affective (an adjective meaning emotional — wrong part of speech here)
effective (means 'producing results' — not the right word)
No error — 'effected' can mean 'influenced'

questions.explanation: A is correct. AFFECT (verb) = to influence or have an impact on. EFFECT (noun) = a result or outcome; (verb, rare) = to bring about. 'She was so AFFECTED (influenced/moved) by the tragedy' — the verb 'affected' is needed. 'Effected' would mean she brought the tragedy into existence — wrong meaning entirely. Affect/effect confusion is the #1 grammar error in English.

questions.stem:
Identify the wrongly used word:

'The eminent arrival of the chief minister was announced by the press office three days before the event.'

options.option_text: imminent (EMINENT=distinguished/famous; IMMINENT=about to happen; here 'about to happen' is the intended meaning)
prominent (means 'important/famous' — similar to EMINENT, but neither fits 'arrival' in this context)
No error — 'eminent' can describe a notable arrival
eminence (noun form — changing part of speech unnecessarily)

questions.explanation: A is correct. EMINENT means distinguished, famous, or respected (describes a person). IMMINENT means about to happen very soon (describes an event). 'The imminent arrival' = the arrival that is about to happen — this is the correct usage. 'The eminent arrival' incorrectly uses the adjective for 'famous' to describe a scheduled event. The replacement: 'The IMMINENT arrival of the chief minister was announced.'

questions.stem:
One word is wrongly used. Choose the correct replacement:

'The government decided to wave the processing fee for first-time applicants of the new scheme.'

options.option_text: waive (WAVE=to move back and forth; WAIVE=to give up a right or refrain from enforcing a rule; 'waive the fee' is the correct phrase)
waver (means to be indecisive or uncertain — wrong context)
No error — 'wave' can mean to waive in informal contexts
withdraw (changes the meaning to removing rather than exempting)

questions.explanation: A is correct. WAIVE = to give up or not enforce a right, claim, or fee (a legal term). The phrase 'waive the processing fee' means to exempt applicants from paying it. WAVE = to move the hand back and forth as a greeting. The sentence needs 'waive.' The wave/waive pair is a frequent word-swap error in competitive English papers.

questions.stem:
Replace the wrongly used word:

'The auditor's report casted serious doubts on the transparency of the company's financial dealings.'

options.option_text: cast (CAST is both present and past tense of 'cast' — 'casted' is non-standard; correct: 'cast serious doubts')
has cast (changes to present perfect — unnecessary tense change)
No error — 'casted' is acceptable in formal English
casting (present participle — wrong for a simple past sentence)

questions.explanation: A is correct. CAST is an irregular verb: cast (present) / cast (past) / cast (past participle). 'Casted' is non-standard and incorrect. The past tense is simply 'cast' — it does not add '-ed'. Correct sentence: 'The auditor's report CAST serious doubts...' Similar irregular verbs: cut/cut, put/put, set/set, bet/bet.

questions.stem:
Identify the wrongly used word:

'The scientist found the results of the experiment to be quite unique and unlike anything she had seen before.'

options.option_text: rather unique (UNIQUE means one of a kind — it cannot be modified by 'quite', 'very', 'somewhat', or 'rather'; it is absolute)
unique (the word 'unique' itself is correct — it means one of a kind; however 'quite unique' is the error since 'unique' is absolute)
quite (the adverb 'quite' is the error; 'unique' is an absolute adjective and cannot be qualified — change to just 'unique')
No error — 'quite unique' is acceptable in modern usage

questions.explanation: C is correct. UNIQUE is an absolute adjective — something either is unique (the only one of its kind) or it isn't. Gradable modifiers like 'quite', 'very', 'somewhat', 'rather', 'more/most' cannot logically modify it. The error is 'quite unique.' Correct: 'The results were unique and unlike anything...' Other absolute adjectives: perfect, dead, infinite, complete, absolute, empty, full. Note: in informal spoken English 'quite unique' is common but grammatically incorrect in formal/exam contexts.

questions.stem:
Replace the wrongly used word:

'The minister's statement was deliberately ambiguous so as to allude scrutiny from the media.'

options.option_text: elude (ALLUDE=to make an indirect reference; ELUDE=to avoid or escape; 'to elude scrutiny' = to avoid scrutiny ✓)
illusion (noun form — wrong part of speech and wrong meaning)
No error — 'allude scrutiny' is grammatically acceptable
allusion (noun form — not a verb, wrong part of speech)

questions.explanation: A is correct. ALLUDE = to make an indirect or passing reference to something ('allude to a scandal'). ELUDE = to escape or avoid ('elude the police'). 'Allude scrutiny' is wrong in meaning — the minister was trying to ESCAPE scrutiny, not refer to it indirectly. Correct: 'to ELUDE scrutiny.' This is a common confusable pair: allude/elude/illusion/allusion all look similar.

questions.stem:
Identify the error and choose the correct word:

'After an exhaustive research, the team published their findings in a peer-reviewed journal.'

options.option_text: exhaustive (EXHAUSTIVE means thorough/comprehensive — this is actually correct here: 'exhaustive research' = thorough research)
an (the article 'an' before 'exhaustive' — 'exhaustive' starts with a vowel sound 'ɛ'; use 'an' before vowel sounds ✓)
No error — the sentence is grammatically correct (exhaustive is correctly used and 'an' before 'exhaustive' is correct)

their (RESEARCH is uncountable and typically treated as singular — 'their findings' is fine if the team is plural; the real error may be 'an exhaustive research' — research is uncountable and does not take 'an')

questions.explanation: D is correct. RESEARCH is an uncountable noun in standard English — it does not take an indefinite article ('a' or 'an'). Correct: 'After exhaustive research...' (no article). 'An exhaustive research' is grammatically wrong. Other uncountable nouns often misused with articles: advice, furniture, information, equipment, luggage. Note: 'exhaustive' itself is correct (= thorough), and 'an' before vowel sounds is grammatically fine, but 'research' being uncountable is the key error.
